source.title: Low-Resource Safety Failures Are Action Failures, Not Representation Failures
source.authors: Rashad Aziz; Ikhlasul Akmal Hanif; Fajri Koto

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It uses the contrastive difference-in-means harmfulness direction and intervenes on it, but tests it at selected layers and in multilingual settings rather than reproducing the original all-layer, all-position intervention. It also evaluates conditional steering and cross-language transfer.
record.gate_note: The paper reports several additional results, including classifier F1, OOD balanced accuracy, steering latency, and comparisons with CAST and AdaSteer. They are not included unless they directly measure the claim versions; cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study builds the Arditi difference-in-means direction from pooled high-resource-language (HRL) activations in three instruct models. Ablating it at one layer at a time, across all positions, drops harmful refusal to near zero or below 15%. Adding it recovers refusal on low-resource-language (LRL) prompts, and its projection still separates harmful from harmless LRL prompts. This is a new multilingual setting with direct results on V1, V5 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Harmfulness stays linearly decodable from the HRL direction in LRLs, but scores shift downward. Ablating or adding the direction changes refusal. Remaining failures split into classifier errors and non-refusals after addition, in model-dependent proportions. A few-shot latent gate raises mean selectivity to 54.5 (vs CAST 33.6) without hurting Global-MMLU.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the contrastive harmful-minus-harmless activation mean direction and residual-stream projection/addition. The direction is pooled across HRLs, interventions are examined at selected extraction layers rather than jointly at every layer and position, and the added/ablated direction is often routed by a learned classifier.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by model, language, resource tier, layer, and steering/calibration setting. The largest ablation effect occurs at model-specific middle layers. Lower-resource tiers require larger addition strength; HRL-only calibration works better for Qwen and Gemma, while Llama benefits from target-language examples. Harmless refusal is notably higher for some conditions, including Yoruba.

fits_no_version.finding: A few-shot-calibrated rank-10 HRL subspace classifier detects LRL harmful prompts (macro F1 ~0.72–0.90; OOD balanced accuracy up to 0.933), beating a random-direction control.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: HRL harmfulness geometry yields a few-shot calibratable multilingual harm classifier.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code is available on GitHub but gives no URL in the text)
record.problems: Only three open dense instruction-tuned 7B–9B models and the studied PolyRefuse languages are tested. Common Crawl share is a coarse resource proxy; much of the multilingual benchmark is translated. Refusal is judged automatically, and the authors report false-positive bias despite a 600-example human audit. The ablation results are given as figure descriptions/bounds rather than exact values. The capability check is GlobalMMLU after conditional steering, not after direct ablation.
record.rows_left_out: Did not include the full per-language base refusal-rate table, every uncalibrated and HRL-only conditional-steering result, adapted CAST/AdaSteer comparison rows, classifier calibration/F1 sweeps, OOD benchmark rows, judge-ablation results, or latency measurements. These are omitted to prioritize direct direction interventions, cross-language representation evidence, refusal outcomes, the refusal-versus-classifier-error decomposition, and the stated capability check. Figure-only AUC values are retained only at the model-level description because exact cells are not stated in the text.

untested.parts: Simultaneous ablation at all layers; adding the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal; capability after ablation (the only utility check is after the conditional gate, at near-chance MMLU).
No separate refusal direction is extracted or compared with the harmfulness direction.
Transfer across base/instruct or other model variants; languages outside PolyRefuse/IndoSafety/MultiJail.
Entire version (the rank-10 subspace is used only for classification).

missing.what: IndoSafety harmful refusal, no intervention vs always adding the direction: Qwen 6.0→71.5, Gemma 14.9→92.7, Llama 16.2→62.4.
Share of all harmful prompts classified harmful yet unrefused after addition: Qwen 25.3%, Gemma 0.6%, Llama 26.2%, Qwen–Amharic 52.1%.
Ablating pooled vHRL vs English ven: vHRL reduces refusal more in Qwen and Gemma, similarly in Llama. Refusal stays high outside the middle-layer band.
Addition sweeps for Gemma and Llama raise harmful refusal, with model- and tier-specific optima.
Cells with high AUC but low base refusal (e.g. Qwen Amharic base refusal 4.4%). This shows harm is decodable while refusal is absent.

record.verdict_notes: Rows r7–r24 and r31–r42 are the authors' own gating method compared with baselines, so they are unlinked. Its MMLU check sits near chance and cannot show capability preservation. The refusal judge overestimates refusal (32 of 45 disagreements are false positives). The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The paper removes the direction one layer at a time, not simultaneously from every layer and position. Harmless-request refusal after unconditional direction addition is not separately reported. General capability is measured after conditional steering, not after the single-direction ablation.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
A rank-10 subspace is used for classification, but the paper does not test whether refusal itself is better described by an affine set, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
The paper distinguishes harmfulness classification from refusal behavior, but does not establish a separate harmfulness and refusal direction or fully characterize their representations.
Tests transfer from pooled HRL activations to LRL prompts in the studied models and languages; does not test transfer across base/instruct variants or languages outside the study.
No comparison of refusal-training procedures, or when refusal was trained.

relationships.condition: Single middle-layer ablation on HRL prompts in Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.1-8B; addition on LRL harmful prompts
relationships.reason: Ablation cuts harmful refusal from 84–95% to near zero or below 15% (r1–r3). Addition recovers LRL refusal (r6); always-intervene on IndoSafety raises refusal 6–16% to 62–93% (text, Table 12).
relationships.display_finding: Ablation reduced harmful refusal from 84–95% to near zero or below 15%, while always-on addition raised IndoSafety refusal from 6–16% to 62–93%.

source_check.notes: The paper's 'harmfulness direction' is the final-token difference-in-means direction, ablated at one layer at a time. Table 3/10 shares are residual failures of the gated method at a fixed lambda: prompts classified harmful get the direction added, those classified harmless get it ablated. Figure 5 AUCs are described only in pooled form. No rows hold the ablation comparison against the English direction (Figure 2), the Gemma and Llama addition sweeps (Figure 20) or the IndoSafety numbers (Table 12).
